summary.headline: Energy, freight and labour rose together through Q2 2026 — the three biggest non-commodity inputs moving in the same direction at once, which is what turns a manageable commodity picture into a margin problem. Crude and diesel corrected off their war peaks in June, but every energy series remains 20-75% above year-ago levels, European gas and power re-accelerated hard in July as the Strait of Hormuz closed again, and container freight ran a peak season that started early. Labour is the slow, structural one: legislated wage floors, not scarcity, and they do not reverse when the conflict does.

pillars.commentary: Crude corrected off its June peak and diesel, jet fuel and bunker fuel followed it down — but only from extraordinary highs, and the annual comparison is unforgiving: Brent is still +20% YoY, German diesel +30%, US jet fuel +47%, Ghent marine gasoil +45%. July then split the market in two. Oil kept easing on hopes of a durable US-Iran settlement, while European gas and power went the other way: TTF +19.2% MoM and the European electricity index +18.7% MoM, as the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz cut Qatari LNG flows into a continent with low storage, and a heatwave lifted cooling demand on top. German baseload power at €124.83/MWh is +74% YoY. For food and beverage processing — drying, chilling, sterilising — this is the input that bites hardest, and it is the one that reversed direction most recently.

drivers.name: Electricity baseload
drivers.source: Iberian Energy Derivatives Exchange, Marex Spectron

pillars.commentary: Peak season arrived early. Frontloading ahead of anticipated new US tariffs, plus carrier peak-season surcharges, pushed the 40ft composite index up 31% MoM by mid-July and 74% above a year ago; Shanghai-Rotterdam moved with it at +31% MoM on tight Asia-Europe capacity. The turn came late in the month — by 31 July the composite had eased to $4,255/unit, down 6.1% from end-June as frontloading faded — but carriers are actively managing capacity to defend rates and have signalled further emergency fuel surcharges for August, so the fall is not yet a trend. Road freight is the quieter, stickier problem: driver shortages, new tolls that took effect on 1 July and elevated diesel keep European road rates grinding up (+11% YoY) with no conflict-driven reversal available.

drivers.name: Ocean container, US East Coast to North Europe

pillars.commentary: Labour is the pillar that does not correct. EU manufacturing labour costs rose 3.3% YoY in Q1 2026 — the slowest in two years, but still ahead of the 2.8% euro-area headline — and the drivers are legislated rather than cyclical: statutory minimum wage floors moved in Germany, the UK, Belgium and the Netherlands within seven months. That matters disproportionately in food and beverage manufacturing, where pay sits below the wider manufacturing average and a large share of the workforce is concentrated near the wage floor, so a floor increase passes through almost one-for-one. EU food-service labour costs still trail manufacturing by roughly 39% in absolute terms, which preserves a structural cost advantage — but it is exactly the advantage that minimum-wage increases erode fastest.

drivers.name: Labour cost, manufacturing
drivers.note: Not seasonally adjusted — the quarterly fall is the usual Q4-to-Q1 bonus effect, not an easing of wage costs.

pillars.commentary: The cost base under packaging, one step before the prices in the Packaging category. Pulp is the pressure point: European eucalyptus BHK rose 4% MoM and 30% YoY on mill closures and capacity cuts, and NBSK added another 1.1% MoM — enough to push European kraftliner up 6.2% MoM in June while the rest of the board complex sat flat. Recovered paper pulls the other way: European corrugated waste is down more than 32% YoY because weak paper production means weak demand for it, capping recycled-grade board. The polymer chain is easing — ethylene, propylene and paraxylene all softened outside the US on oversupply in Asia and Europe — but naphtha remains hostage to the Strait of Hormuz, so the resin relief that started in May is only as durable as the ceasefire.

actions.label: Reprice energy surcharges now, not at renewal
actions.body: European gas and power turned back up in July (TTF +19.2% MoM, EU electricity index +18.7% MoM) after a two-month fall, and German baseload is +74% YoY. Suppliers on energy-linked clauses will pass this through with a lag; ask for the indexation formula and the reference month before the next invoice cycle, and challenge any surcharge still anchored to the June peak in crude, which has since eased.

actions.label: Use the freight window, but do not extrapolate it
actions.body: The 40ft composite eased 6.1% from end-June to $4,255/unit by 31 July as frontloading faded — the first genuine break after an early peak season. Carriers are managing capacity to defend rates and have flagged August emergency fuel surcharges, so treat this as a booking window for Q3 volumes rather than evidence of a downtrend. Asia-Europe is the tight leg: Shanghai-Rotterdam is still +46% YoY.

actions.label: Treat wage floors as permanent, and renegotiate labour-heavy scopes
actions.body: Minimum wage increases in Germany (+8.4%), the UK (+4.1%), Belgium and the Netherlands are legislated and will not unwind with the conflict. Labour-intensive scopes — packing, handling, chilled logistics, catering services — carry a structural cost step that suppliers will seek to recover. Ask for the labour share of cost in any repricing request and index only that share, rather than accepting a blended increase across the whole contract.
